turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Morning. I'm Dr Okonkwo. Have a seat — what's been going on?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Hi. Um, it's my heart. It keeps racing, and I get really breathless with it.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): When you say racing, what does it feel like?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): A flutter, sort of. Well, actually, sometimes it just pounds. I don't know, doctor, it's hard to describe.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Does the breathlessness come on with the racing?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. I can't get a proper breath in. My partner's noticed too — she says I'm breathing all quick when I'm half asleep, and she can feel my chest going.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): How long has this been happening?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): The heart racing and the breathlessness? I don't know, doctor. A few months, maybe from around the new year, but I couldn't give you a date. It crept up.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Is it there all the time, or in spells?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Spells. Most nights, worse when I'm trying to sleep.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): And through the day?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Before exams, and before meetings at work. That's the awkward bit.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): You're doing exams and a job?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Final year, and a part-time job in the shop office, so yeah, meetings. It's a lot, but I'm fine. Bus was late again, mind, I'm still flustered from standing about.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Around the exams and the meetings, do you feel stressed, or anxious?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor. I don't think I'm stressed. I wouldn't call it stress. People always jump to that.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain with these spells?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No pain. Just the thumping and the breathlessness.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Have you ever blacked out, or felt you were about to faint?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No, never. I stay awake through it. I do get a bit shaky when it's bad, though.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): How often, roughly, and how long does a spell go on?

[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Most nights, worse when I'm trying to get to sleep, and a couple of times in the day before an exam or a meeting. It fades on its own — about ten minutes, sometimes longer. I don't know exactly, I haven't timed it.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): What are you drinking in the day?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Coffee. Loads. Five mugs — well, actually, more like six. And energy drinks, the big cans, about two a day when I'm revising.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Not cigarettes. I vape, though. Since uni. A pod every couple of days, give or take.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any medicines at the moment?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Not now. I was on propranolol, the little tablets, but I stopped it in March.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do you remember the dose, and how often you were taking it?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): I think it was 10 milligrams, once a day. I don't know, doctor, it might've been that. It was for the palpitations.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): What made you stop?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): It left me feeling a bit flat, and I wasn't sure it helped, so I packed it in. Not had one since.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Was anything else suggested that you didn't take?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Sertraline. The GP wrote it and I never started it. Wasn't keen on the idea.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any asthma, any thyroid problems, any heart trouble in the past?
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing like that. I've always been pretty healthy, touch wood.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll check your pulse and blood pressure, and have a listen.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Go on, then. Those magazines out there are ancient, by the way. Felt like 2014 in the waiting room.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): Pulse is 92, and it's regular. Blood pressure is 124 over 76. Oxygen sats 98 percent.
[SEG0040] person_1 (DOCTOR): Heart sounds are normal, there's no murmur, and your chest is clear.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Is 92 bad? I don't know, doctor. Sounds high for just sitting here.
[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): It's a touch quick for resting, but the rhythm is regular, and the rest of the examination is reassuring.

[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me summarise. For a few months you've had spells of a fluttering or pounding heart with breathlessness, worse at night and before exams or meetings. No chest pain, no blackouts. You vape, you're on a lot of coffee and energy drinks, you stopped propranolol in March, and you never started the sertraline. You don't see it as stress.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, that's about right. I still couldn't tell you when it actually started, though.
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): We can leave the exact start date. It doesn't change the plan for today.

[SEG0046] person_1 (DOCTOR): My working impression is that this is most likely palpitations driven by the caffeine, and by the run-up to exams and meetings, even if it doesn't feel like stress to you. I can't rule out an abnormal heart rhythm, or an overactive thyroid, until we've checked.
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): Thyroid. Alright. Hadn't crossed my mind, if I'm honest.
[SEG0048] person_1 (DOCTOR): That's why we look. I'd like a blood test for your thyroid, and an ECG today to see the rhythm.
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): Does the ECG hurt? Sorry, that's a daft question.
[SEG0050] person_1 (DOCTOR): Not daft, and no, it doesn't hurt. Just stickers on the chest for a minute. The blood test is one quick needle.
[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay. I can manage that.

[SEG0052] person_1 (DOCTOR): In the meantime, ease off the energy drinks and cut the coffee down. Vaping can nudge the pulse up as well, so less of that would help. When a spell starts, try slow breathing — in through the nose for four, and out for six, for a few minutes.
[SEG0053] person_2 (PATIENT): I'll have a go. I don't know if I'll remember once it's actually happening.

[SEG0054] person_1 (DOCTOR): Even a couple of cycles is worth it. If you get chest pain, if you faint, or if the breathlessness is severe and not settling, go straight to A&E rather than waiting to see me.
[SEG0055] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, understood.
[SEG0056] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll see you back in two weeks with the results. Reception will book it as you leave.
[SEG0057] person_2 (PATIENT): Two weeks. Okay.
[SEG0058] person_1 (DOCTOR): Anything you wanted to ask before you head off?
[SEG0059] person_2 (PATIENT): Um, I don't think so. I don't know, doctor, I think we've covered it.
[SEG0060] person_1 (DOCTOR): Good. We'll get those tests done on the way out, then.

spec.situation: Young adult with palpitations and breathlessness, worse at night and before exams or work meetings; downplays stress, drinks a lot of coffee and energy drinks, vapes; friend or partner contributes. Doctor orders ECG and thyroid tests, discusses breathing exercises.
features: doctor_misses_topics: the doctor does not ask about everything; topics never discussed are simply absent (no invented denials, no allergy line if allergies were never mentioned).

stopped_or_never_taken: a medicine the patient stopped, was never given or only took once ('I stopped it in March'). Status discontinued, not current; a medicine never taken is not recorded as a medication.

omissions.text: Patient said the breathlessness feels like they 'can't get a proper breath in.'
Partner has noticed the patient breathing quickly when half asleep and can feel the patient's chest moving during these episodes.
Patient stopped propranolol because it made them feel 'a bit flat' and they were not sure it helped; they have not taken any since stopping.
Sertraline was prescribed by the GP but never started because the patient was not keen on the idea.
Recorded fact 'Stress or anxiety absent' is misleading: the patient said they do not think they are stressed and would not call it stress, rather than a definite absence of stress/anxiety.
